tour.title: Annapurna Base Camp: The Sanctuary Trek
tour.summary: Eleven days from a lakeside town to a glacial amphitheatre at 4,130 metres: stone stairs, rhododendron forest, Gurung and Magar villages, and the 8,091-metre peak that cost the first men to climb an eight-thousander their fingers and toes.
tour.overviewText:
Somewhere ahead of you is a hole in the mountains, and the only way in is a gorge so narrow it feels like a mistake.

That hole is the Annapurna Sanctuary: a glacial basin 40 km north of Pokhara, an oval of glacier, moraine and grass above 4,000 metres, ringed by peaks that are almost all over 7,000. The range it sits inside is 55 km long and holds one eight-thousander, Annapurna I at 8,091 metres, the tenth-highest mountain on Earth, plus thirteen peaks over 7,000. Annapurna means 'the giver of food', the goddess of nourishment, named for the rivers that run off these glaciers and water the plains below. West of it, across the Kali Gandaki, stands Dhaulagiri, the white mountain, at 8,167 metres. The river between the two is often called the deepest gorge on Earth.

For most of history the sanctuary was not a destination but a taboo. The Gurung, the Tibeto-Burman people whose villages you will walk through, held it sacred: a storehouse of gold left by the naga, the serpent-gods, and the home of deities older than either Hinduism or Buddhism. Machhapuchhre, the fishtail peak at the entrance, was Shiva's seat, and the plume of snow blowing off its summit was his incense. Eggs and meat were traditionally forbidden inside the basin, and women were not allowed in at all. The first outsider on record to reach it was a British colonel, Jimmy Roberts, in 1956; he called the approach 'dismal bamboo slogging' and named the place the Sanctuary.

Six years earlier, in 1950, Maurice Herzog and Louis Lachenal had climbed Annapurna I, the first 8,000-metre peak ever climbed, and come down with frostbitten hands and feet. Herzog lost all his fingers and toes; Lachenal lost his toes. The mountain kept its reputation: by one count, it has killed roughly one climber for every five who have reached the top. Your route goes to the base of that face, not up it.

Nepal packs its middle hills with people, and this walk is a tour of how they live. The Gurung and the Magar, the two Tibeto-Burman peoples of these hills, farm terraces of millet, maize and potatoes and send sons into the Gurkha regiments, the Nepali soldiers Britain and India have recruited since the Anglo-Nepalese War of 1814 to 1816. Since the 1970s the other crop has been trekkers. The trail is a chain of teahouses, family lodges with a dining room, a stove and a menu built around dal bhat, the rice-and-lentil plate that is Nepal's daily fuel. The upper valley runs on porters, guides, mule trains and the ACAP permit you bought in Pokhara; the Annapurna Conservation Area Project runs the protected area and pays for its trail crews through that permit.

The shape of the walk is a long approach and a short, steep entrance. You start on the shore of Phewa Lake in Pokhara, climb through terraced fields and rhododendron forest to Poon Hill for sunrise, drop into the Modi Khola gorge, follow it up between Hiunchuli and Machhapuchhre into the sanctuary, and come back down the same valley to hot springs beside the river.

Practicals. This is an eleven-day trip with eight walking days, about 85 kilometres, four to seven hours a day. The high point is 4,130 metres, and on the last two days up it is altitude, not distance, that sets the pace. You need an ACAP permit, NPR 3,000 for foreigners at the time of writing. Nepal also began requiring a licensed guide on these routes in 2023. Carry cash: there are no ATMs above Pokhara, and lodges charge separately for hot showers, charging and Wi-Fi. Come in spring, March to May, for the rhododendrons, or in autumn, late September to November, for clear air; the monsoon closes the views and opens the leeches. Prices and rules move, so verify at the counter rather than on a blog.

Then go and stand in the hole.
tour.difficulty: Hard. Eight walking days of four to seven hours, roughly 85 km in total, with thousands of stone steps, repeated 500-metre climbs and descents, and a high point of 4,130 metres at Annapurna Base Camp. No technical climbing and no ropes, but the altitude is the real difficulty: the itinerary gains 1,240 metres on the day it reaches base camp, which is fast, and altitude sickness is a genuine risk above 3,000 metres. Knees take a beating on the descents, and the trail is rough, wet and exposed in places.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start before seven every morning, and before five on the Poon Hill day. The mountains are clearest at dawn, the cloud builds by mid-morning, and afternoon rain or snow is normal even in season. The one fixed appointment is Annapurna Base Camp at sunrise, when the light hits Annapurna South and then Annapurna I; the second is Poon Hill, forty-five minutes above Ghorepani, where you want to be standing in the dark before the sun comes up.
tour.imageCredits: Photographs are bundled from Wikimedia Commons under public domain or Creative Commons licences. Full attribution for each image appears on its stop page and in Settings.

stops.name: Phewa Lake, Pokhara
stops.narration:
Stand at the lake's edge and look north. That wall of white is 25 to 40 kilometres away and it looks close enough to hit with a stone, because of the arithmetic of the Himalaya: Machhapuchhre's summit is 6,993 metres and the valley you are standing in is 820, so the mountain gains six vertical kilometres in about twenty-five horizontal ones. On a clear morning, before ten and before the haze, you can see Dhaulagiri on the left, the Annapurnas in the middle and Machhapuchhre's double summit on the right, a row that includes three of the ten highest mountains on Earth.

Pokhara is Nepal's second city and the capital of Gandaki Province, a green basin of roughly half a million people that lives on three things: tourism, remittances from abroad, and the pensions of Gurkha soldiers. The lake, Phewa, is the second-largest in Nepal. It is fed by streams off the Annapurnas and held back by a small dam at its southern end, which is why the water level is steady enough for the boats that ferry pilgrims and tourists out to Talbarahi, the two-tiered pagoda on the island. The lake is also filling with silt, slowly, the way all Himalayan lakes do.

What matters for the next ten days is that this is the shopfront. The strip along the eastern shore is one long gear shop, lodge and trekking agency, and the permit offices are here too. Buy or rent what you are missing, draw enough cash for the whole trek, and check your boots now rather than at 3,000 metres. Then look north again, because the mountain you can see on a clear morning is the one whose base you are going to walk to.

One local word before you go: himal means snow, and the range in front of you is the abode of snow. The people who live under it have a more practical relationship with it than the postcards suggest. They farm the terraces, herd goats, and go where the work is. For the last fifty years, much of that work has been walking other people up these valleys.
stops.entranceFeeNote: The lakeshore is free. Boats to the Talbarahi temple and the World Peace Pagoda charge a few hundred rupees, and the ACAP permit for the trek costs NPR 3,000 for foreigners, bought in Pokhara or online; verify the current fee at the counter.
stops.openingHours: The lakeshore is open at all hours. Shops, agencies and permit offices run roughly 9am to 6pm, and the permit office closes at weekends and public holidays, so do not leave it to the morning you leave.
stops.accessibility: The lakeside road and pavement are flat and step-free, though the strip is busy with motorbikes and the lakefront path is uneven in places. Boats and the temple island are not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: The mountain view is a dawn view. The haze builds by mid-morning and the peaks vanish by afternoon, so set an alarm for first light and walk to the north end of the lake, where the water is still and the reflection works. Then go and buy your permit.
stops.nextStopDirections: Day 2 is a road day, not a walk. Leave Pokhara early on the Baglung Highway, about 1.5 to 2 hours and 35 km to Nayapul, then on to Birethanti, where the ACAP checkpoint is. The approach drive is not counted in this tour's walking total; the trek's own distances begin at the permit gate.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Gaurav Dhwaj Khadka, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Birethanti: The Permit Gate
stops.narration:
Two rivers meet here, and the checkpoint sits at the junction. The Modi Khola comes down from the sanctuary you are heading for; the Bhurungdi Khola comes down from the Ghorepani side; khola means river, and you will hear the word all week. They join, and the combined river turns south towards the plains. Birethanti grew up as a rest stop on the old trade route, and thanti means a resting place, the same word you will meet again at Banthanti and Nangethanti. Its stone houses and tea shops have been serving people with loads on their backs for a long time.

The ACAP counter is why you stop. The Annapurna Conservation Area is 7,629 square kilometres, Nepal's largest protected area and the first of its kind here. Instead of a national park run by soldiers, it is managed by the National Trust for Nature Conservation with the villages inside it, and your NPR 3,000 permit pays for trail crews, rubbish collection, kerosene depots and these checkpoints. The rules are real: no firewood above Chhomrong, no hunting, no drones without permission, and a double fee if you turn up at a checkpost without a permit. The register also tells rescuers who is up the valley.

Look at the bridge and the water. The Modi Khola is glacial melt, milky with rock flour ground off the Annapurna glaciers, which is why it runs grey-green rather than blue. The old route from here climbed on foot up the Bhurungdi Khola; now a jeep track runs up the valley to Tikhedhunga, and most groups drive it. That is the honest shape of this trek today: the bottom of the trail has a road on it. The walking starts where the road runs out.
stops.entranceFeeNote: The ACAP permit is NPR 3,000 for foreign nationals, NPR 1,000 for SAARC nationals and free for children under 10. Buy it in Pokhara or online before you arrive: permits issued at a checkpost cost double. Verify the rate when you buy, and carry the printed copy.
stops.openingHours: The checkpoint is staffed through the trekking day in season, roughly 7am to 5pm. Outside those hours there may be nobody to register you, which is another reason to arrive early.
stops.accessibility: The checkpoint and bridge are reached from the road on a short, uneven stone path with a few steps. The suspension bridge itself is narrow and moves underfoot; not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Register even if nobody asks. The ACAP register is the record of who is above Chhomrong, and it is the one rescue teams reach for when the weather turns. Carry a passport copy and a pen; the form is quicker than the queue.
stops.nextStopDirections: From Birethanti the jeep track follows the Bhurungdi Khola upstream for about 6 to 7 km to Tikhedhunga, 30 to 40 minutes by vehicle. On foot the same stretch is 1.5 to 2 hours along a dusty road with little shade. The itinerary drives it, then starts walking at the bottom of the staircase.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Gerd Eichmann, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Tikhedhunga: The Bottom of the Stairs
stops.narration:
This is the bottom of the staircase. The village sits at about 1,540 metres on the Bhurungdi Khola, and the trail leaving the far bank is not really a trail. It is a staircase: over three thousand stone steps climbing roughly five hundred metres in two and a half kilometres to Ulleri. Nobody agrees on the count. You will hear 3,000, 3,200, 3,300 and occasionally 3,700, because the staircase is not one flight but a series of flights patched and rebuilt over generations, and because counting steps is what people do instead of breathing.

The steps are local stone, laid dry or in mud mortar, and they exist because this hillside is too steep and too wet for a dirt path to survive a monsoon. The same stone is under the houses: schist and gneiss, metamorphic rock squeezed and folded by the collision that is still building the Himalaya. Every kilogram of rice, cement, beer and gas cylinder in the villages above comes up these steps on a mule or a human back, which is why a bottle of water costs more the higher you go.

Mule trains use the staircase too, bells first. When you hear them, step to the uphill side and stand still; a loaded mule will not stop and cannot swerve on a step. The first twenty minutes are the worst, then your breathing settles into a rhythm and the steps become a kind of metronome. Do not race the porters. They are carrying twenty kilos and they will still beat you to the top.

At the top, Ulleri's lodges sell lemon ginger honey, which is the correct local medicine whether or not it does anything clinically.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk. Tea and snacks at the lodges cost a few hundred rupees; the lemon ginger honey is worth it. Verify prices on the menu before ordering.
stops.openingHours: The trail is open at all hours, but start the staircase before mid-morning so you are not climbing in the heat of the day.
stops.accessibility: Honestly, no. This is a continuous staircase with uneven risers, no handrail for long stretches and mule traffic. Hiking poles help, and so do knees that have been warned.
stops.insiderTip: Fill your water here and use the toilet. There is nothing on the staircase itself, and the climb takes most people one and a half to two and a half hours. If a mule train passes, stand on the uphill side and let it by.
stops.nextStopDirections: Cross the suspension bridge out of Tikhedhunga and follow the stone staircase uphill without a single flat stretch. It is about 2.5 km and 500 metres of climbing to Ulleri, one and a half to two and a half hours at a sensible pace. Start early; the steps are in shade for part of the morning and in full sun by midday.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Bijay Chaurasia, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Ulleri
stops.narration:
Ulleri is a Magar village at about 1,960 metres, and after the staircase it feels like a reward. The Magar are one of Nepal's oldest indigenous groups, with their own language and their own shamans, and like the Gurung they have served for two centuries in the Gurkha regiments of the British and Indian armies. The money from those pensions is visible: the big stone houses with carved windows, the slate roofs, the school. The smaller houses are older and simpler, and the terraces around them grow maize, millet and potatoes.

Look north. Annapurna South is 7,219 metres, Hiunchuli is 6,441, and for the first time on this walk the mountains are not a backdrop but a presence. The village sits on a ridge, so the view is open on both sides: terraces falling away below, forest above, and the white wall of the Annapurnas across the valley. The air is thinner here, though not yet thin enough to matter; you are at two thousand metres, and the altitude only becomes a real subject above 3,000.

This is also the first place to see how the trek is supplied. A lodge room costs a few hundred rupees a night; the money is made on food, hot showers, charging sockets and beer. Everything arrives on a back or a mule, and the price rises with the distance from the road. That is not a scam, it is a freight bill. The same economics will follow you to base camp.

The village's main street is a staircase, and the lodge terraces face the mountains. Sit down, order dal bhat, and watch the light change on Annapurna South.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk through. A room in a teahouse is typically a few hundred rupees and meals a few hundred more, with hot showers and charging charged separately; prices rise with altitude, so check the menu and the extras before you settle.
stops.openingHours: The village is inhabited all year, but lodges outside the trekking seasons may close or run with a skeleton staff. The walking day runs from first light to dusk.
stops.accessibility: Stone lanes, steps between houses and uneven terraces. Not step-free, and the village itself is built on a slope.
stops.insiderTip: Walk to the top of the village in the late afternoon. The view of Annapurna South and Hiunchuli from above the last lodge is better than from any terrace, and the sunset light is the reason to stop here rather than push on.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave Ulleri on the trail above the village and follow the ridge through oak and rhododendron forest. It is about 9 km and four hours to Ghorepani, with a steady climb past the rest houses at Banthanti and Nangethanti. The forest is the point: in spring the rhododendrons are in flower, and in autumn the oaks turn.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Gerd Eichmann, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Ghorepani: Horse Water
stops.narration:
Ghorepani means horse water: ghora, horse, and pani, water. This ridge was a watering stop on the salt route between the lowlands and Tibet, where caravans of mules and horses rested and drank before the long climb. The trade died when roads reached the valleys, and the village reinvented itself as a teahouse stop. The blue roofs are the giveaway: this is a village built for trekkers, not for caravans, though a few old troughs survive at the southern end if you look for them.

The forest around you is the other reason people come. Oak and rhododendron, moss on everything, and in April the rhododendrons flower red and pink. Rhododendron is Nepal's national flower, lali gurans, and the Annapurna region is one of its strongholds. The trees also supply the lodges with firewood; above Chhomrong, where the sanctuary begins, firewood is banned and the lodges run on kerosene and solar instead.

Ghorepani is Pun Magar country. Pun is a Magar clan, and Poon Hill is their hill, not a misspelling of the English word. The village is in two parts, lower and upper, and the ACAP checkpoint sits between them. At 2,860 metres you may notice the altitude in your sleep: the breathing pauses that wake you, the dry throat, the strange dreams. That is normal. Drink water, skip the beer, and keep the next morning's climb to Poon Hill slow.

Upper Ghorepani has the better view of the Dhaulagiri range, and the 'Welcome to Ghorepani Poon Hill' archway, which is the photograph everyone takes and nobody needs.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk through. Teahouse rooms and meals are priced higher than at Ulleri because everything is carried further; hot showers and charging are extra. Verify the extras before you agree to the room.
stops.openingHours: The village runs through the trekking seasons; outside them many lodges close. The checkpoint is staffed during daylight hours.
stops.accessibility: Stone-paved lanes with steps, and the village is on a ridge with steep side paths. Not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Walk up to upper Ghorepani for sunset, then eat early and sleep. The Poon Hill climb starts before five, and the lodge kitchens open early enough for tea but not for a proper breakfast; eat breakfast when you come back down.
stops.nextStopDirections: The Poon Hill path leaves from the upper village and climbs through rhododendron forest for about 45 minutes to an hour, roughly 1.5 km and 350 metres of ascent. Everyone walks it in the dark with a headlamp to be on top for sunrise, and everyone comes back down the same way for breakfast.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Samir and Dipak Tamang from Kathmandu, Nepal, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Poon Hill Sunrise
stops.narration:
Three thousand two hundred and ten metres, and the whole Annapurna and Dhaulagiri ranges lined up like a theatre set. The reason the view works is the Kali Gandaki gorge: the river has cut between Dhaulagiri and Annapurna I, and the result is often called the deepest gorge on Earth, five and a half vertical kilometres from the river to the summits, with the peaks only 30 or 40 kilometres apart. From here you are looking across that gap.

The list, left to right: Dhaulagiri I at 8,167 metres, the seventh-highest mountain on Earth; Annapurna I at 8,091, the tenth; Annapurna South at 7,219; Hiunchuli at 6,441; Nilgiri at 7,061; Tukuche at 6,920; Gangapurna at 7,455; Annapurna III at 7,555; and Machhapuchhre at 6,993, the fishtail, closer than the rest. The sun comes up to your right in the east, so the peaks light from the side rather than the front, and the first colour is a dull rose that turns to gold and then to white. That is alpenglow, and it is real physics: at a low sun angle the light travels through more atmosphere, the blue is scattered out, and the red reaches you.

The name is Pun, not Poon. Pun is a Magar clan, and the hill is theirs. By sunrise the viewing tower and the steps below it are crowded with people in down jackets, which is the price of a view this famous. If you want it quieter, watch from the slope just below the tower rather than fighting for the platform.

And then look east, past the peaks, at the light coming. The mountains have been doing this for millions of years; the crowd is new.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. There is no gate and no ticket, only the ACAP permit you already carry. Tea at the top is sold from a small stall in season; bring small notes.
stops.openingHours: Open at all hours, but the point is dawn. Arrive 30 minutes before sunrise, and carry a headlamp for the climb and a warm layer for the wait.
stops.accessibility: A steep stone and dirt path with tree roots, uneven steps and no handrail for much of the way. Not step-free, and the last stretch to the tower is rough.
stops.insiderTip: Do not sprint up. You are at 3,200 metres before sunrise, and the climb is the first place on this trek where the altitude will make you stop. Walk slowly, breathe through your nose, and give yourself an extra fifteen minutes.
stops.nextStopDirections: Come back down to Ghorepani for breakfast, then take the ridge trail east over the Deurali pass. It is about 11.5 km and four to six hours to Tadapani, with a climb to the pass, a long descent through oak and rhododendron, and a final pull up to the village. The path is muddy after rain and the stone steps are slippery.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Aditya Pal, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Tadapani
stops.narration:
Tadapani means far water: tada, far, and pani, water. Until 2012 the village's drinking water came up from a spring 45 minutes downhill, carried by porters, and the name was a daily complaint. Pipes fixed it; the name stayed. It is a good name for a village on a ridge, because every settlement in these hills is sited by a spring, and the water is almost always below.

The view is the reason people stop. Machhapuchhre's double summit fills the sky to the north, close enough to see the two prongs and the steep north ridge between them, with Annapurna South behind and to the left. The village sits at about 2,630 metres on a saddle where two ridges meet: to the east the ground falls into the Modi Khola, to the west it climbs back towards Poon Hill.

The forest is oak, rhododendron and moss, and it is loud with birds. The one to look for is the danphe, the Himalayan monal, Nepal's national bird: the male is iridescent green and blue with a copper back and a long crest, and he is more often heard scratching than seen. Black-faced laughing thrushes shout from the undergrowth, and grey langurs, the long-tailed monkeys, move through the canopy in troops. In April the forest floor is red with fallen rhododendron petals, and locals call it lali guras ko baraf, rhododendron snow.

The walk here from Ghorepani went over a deurali, a pass with a small shrine, then down through forest so thick that the views come in flashes. That is the pattern for the next two days: climb to a ridge, lose the view in the trees, find it again.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk through. The lodges here are small and family-run; rooms and meals are a few hundred rupees each, with hot showers extra. Verify before you take the room.
stops.openingHours: The village runs through the trekking seasons and closes down in the monsoon and deep winter. The walking day is daylight only.
stops.accessibility: A forest ridge with stone steps, mud and roots; the village lanes are steep. Not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Ask for a room on the north side and set an alarm for sunrise. Machhapuchhre is close enough here that you can watch the summit light up from the lodge terrace without leaving your tea.
stops.nextStopDirections: The trail to Chhomrong drops east off the ridge to the village of Chuile, descends through mossy rhododendron and oak to the Kimrong Khola, crosses it on a suspension bridge, then climbs to Gurjung and Durbin Danda before the long stone staircase up to Chhomrong. It is about 10 km and five hours, with several steep descents and one long climb at the end.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Gerd Eichmann, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Chhomrong: The Last Village
stops.narration:
Chhomrong is the last real village before the sanctuary, and it is built on a staircase. At about 2,170 metres, the village is stacked on a spur above the Modi Khola, with two thousand-odd steps running through it from the river below to the upper lanes, and another set dropping towards the valley on the far side. Houses are stone with slate roofs, whitewashed, with carved windows, and the terraces around them grow millet, maize and potatoes. The name is variously translated as 'place of stone' or 'place of many birds'; the stone version fits what you walk on.

This is Gurung country. The Gurung call themselves Tamu, speak a Tibeto-Burman language, and bury their dead with lamas while their shamans, the Ghyabri and the Pachyu, handle healing and the older gods. Their religion is a layer cake: pre-Buddhist Bon, the old Tibetan religion, Buddhism, shamanic practice and Hindu influence, all in the same village. Tamu Lhosar, their new year, falls in December or January. The big houses with the ornate windows are often the houses of retired Gurkhas, and the remittances that built them are the reason Chhomrong looks prosperous compared with the hamlets above.

Practically, this is the dividing line. Below it, the trail is a chain of villages with farms and schools. Above it, the lodges are seasonal, firewood is banned, and the valley narrows into the gorge. The ACAP checkpoint here is the main one before the sanctuary, and this is the last place to buy anything you have forgotten.

Look up the valley: Machhapuchhre's fishtail, Annapurna South, Hiunchuli. You will see those peaks from the other side in two days.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk through. Lodges here are comfortable for the altitude, with hot showers and charging for a fee; this is also the last place with a reasonable shop, so stock up on snacks and cash.
stops.openingHours: The village is inhabited year-round, but some lodges close in the monsoon. The checkpoint is staffed during daylight in season.
stops.accessibility: Stone steps everywhere, steep lanes between lodges and no step-free route through the village. This is the most stepped settlement on the trek.
stops.insiderTip: Do not arrive at Chhomrong already exhausted. The last climb up from the Chhomrong Khola is a long stone staircase in full sun, and the lodge terraces are worth arriving with enough energy to enjoy. Leave Tadapani early.
stops.nextStopDirections: From Chhomrong the trail drops about 500 metres on stone steps to the Chhomrong Khola, crosses a suspension bridge, then climbs just as steeply to Sinuwa. Beyond Sinuwa it follows the ridge and drops into the bamboo corridor to Bamboo hamlet, about 6 to 7 km and three to four hours in total. The steps down are harder on the knees than the climb.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Nirojsedhai, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Bamboo
stops.narration:
Bamboo is exactly what it says. The hamlet sits at about 2,310 metres in a corridor of bamboo, and the plant is everywhere: tall, hollow, green, growing in dense clumps that close over the trail. This is a cloud forest, permanently damp, with moss on every branch, ferns on the ground and orchids on the trees. The bamboo is also the reason this valley was so hard to enter. It grows back faster than it can be cut, it is slippery when wet, and it hides the trail. Jimmy Roberts, the first outsider to reach the sanctuary in 1956, described the approach as 'dismal bamboo slogging', and you can see why.

The Modi Khola is below you, milky with glacial silt. The gorge it has cut is the only door into the sanctuary, a slot between Hiunchuli and Machhapuchhre, and everything that goes in or out passes through this corridor: trekkers, porters, mules, rice, kerosene, beer, and the rubbish coming back down. Look at the loads on the porters' backs and you understand the price of a plate of dal bhat at 4,000 metres.

The wildlife is here even if you do not see it. Danphe scratch in the undergrowth, grey langurs move in troops, Himalayan tahr, the shaggy mountain goats, work the cliffs above the treeline, and red pandas, which depend on bamboo, live in these forests at low density. In the monsoon the leeches come out, which is one of the reasons the trekking seasons are spring and autumn. The other reason is the rain: June to September brings most of the annual total, and the trail closes under landslides.

Bamboo is a lunch stop on the way up and a bed on the way down. Both are correct.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk through. This is a small cluster of lodges with a limited menu; prices are higher than Chhomrong because everything is carried up the gorge. Verify before ordering.
stops.openingHours: The lodges run through the trekking seasons and are much quieter in the monsoon. The trail is walkable at all hours but should not be attempted in the dark.
stops.accessibility: A narrow forest trail with roots, mud, stone steps and several stream crossings. Not step-free, and leeches are a real nuisance in the wet season.
stops.insiderTip: Keep your boots and socks out of the undergrowth and check your legs when you stop. In the monsoon, gaiters and a little salt on the boots help. The lodge here makes a good garlic soup, which is the local cold remedy.
stops.nextStopDirections: From Bamboo the trail follows the Modi Khola upstream, climbing through bamboo and forest with several waterfalls crossing the path. It is about 5 km and two to three hours to Himalaya, where the gorge narrows and the lodges sit on a shelf above the river.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: MarijaGrujovska, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Himalaya
stops.narration:
The name is bigger than the place. Himalaya is a cluster of lodges at about 2,920 metres, a shelf of flat ground on the side of the gorge. You know the word by now: the abode of snow. Up here it stops being a range on a map and becomes the ground you are walking on.

The gorge has narrowed to a slot. The Modi Khola is a white noise below, the walls are dark gneiss and schist, and water comes off the cliffs in threads that become waterfalls after rain. This is the metamorphic rock the range is built from, pushed up and folded by the Indian plate sliding under Asia; the river has cut down through it as the mountains rose, which is why the valley is so steep and so narrow.

The trail from Bamboo crossed several of those waterfalls and one stretch where the path runs under an overhang. The next day brings the two landmarks everyone talks about: Hinku Cave, a natural shelter used by shepherds and early expeditions, and the Weeping Wall, a cliff that drips meltwater all day and freezes into a curtain in winter. Both are beautiful and both are dangerous: rockfall and ice fall are real, and the rule is to keep moving and not shelter underneath.

Himalaya is where the forest starts to thin. Tonight is the last night with trees around the lodge. Above this, the valley is grass, rock, snow and the avalanche paths that keep it open.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk through. The lodges here are basic and the menu short; a room and three meals will cost more than at Bamboo, and hot water may be a bucket. Verify what is included.
stops.openingHours: The lodges operate in the trekking seasons and close in winter and monsoon. The trail is daylight only above this point.
stops.accessibility: A rough trail with rock steps, stream crossings and exposed sections beside the river. Not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Fill your water bottles at the lodge and treat the water. The streams look clean and are not; everything above here drains villages, lodges and grazing land. Iodine or a filter is worth the weight.
stops.nextStopDirections: Continue up the gorge for about 4 km and two to three hours to Deurali. The trail passes Hinku Cave and the Weeping Wall, then climbs through the last trees to the hamlet at 3,230 metres. Watch the cliffs above the path and do not stop under the ice.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Josep M. Gracia, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Deurali: The Treeline Ends
stops.narration:
You met the word at the pass above Ghorepani: a deurali is a ridge with a shrine, where travellers stop and make an offering. This one is at 3,230 metres, and it is where the trees give up. Below you are rhododendron, oak and bamboo; above, grass, rock, snow and the avalanche paths that keep the upper valley clear of forest.

You passed the valley's two landmarks on the way. Hinku Cave is a natural overhang big enough to shelter a party, and it was used by shepherds and by early expeditions before the lodges existed. The Weeping Wall is a cliff that drips meltwater all day and turns into a curtain of ice in winter. Both are on avalanche and rockfall ground, so the local rule is keep moving and do not shelter underneath.

Now the altitude, because this is where it starts to matter. At 3,230 metres the air pressure is roughly two-thirds of what it is at sea level, so every breath takes in about two-thirds of the oxygen. Your body compensates by breathing faster and by making more red blood cells, which takes days, not hours. Acute mountain sickness feels like a hangover: headache, nausea, dizziness, poor sleep. It is common and usually mild. The emergencies are HACE, fluid on the brain, which brings confusion and stumbling, and HAPE, fluid in the lungs, which brings breathlessness at rest and a cough. The treatment for both is descent, quickly, not a pill. Acetazolamide can help with the symptoms and is not a substitute for going down.

Tomorrow the itinerary climbs 1,240 metres to base camp in one day, which is fast. If you have a bad headache here, sleep lower and see how you feel in the morning. The mountain is not going anywhere.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk through. There are a couple of lodges and a small shop; prices are high because everything is portered. Cash only, and no ATMs since Pokhara.
stops.openingHours: The lodges run in season only. Above Deurali the trail is exposed and should be walked in daylight; afternoon cloud and snow are common.
stops.accessibility: A rough alpine trail with rock steps, loose scree and avalanche debris. Not step-free, and the altitude makes even flat ground hard work.
stops.insiderTip: Sleep here only if you feel well. The jump from 2,920 metres at Himalaya to 4,130 at base camp is the classic altitude trap; if you are headachey or nauseous, stay at Deurali or go down, and do not take a headache up the mountain.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the trees behind and follow the trail across open slopes to Machhapuchhre Base Camp, about 4 km and two to three hours. The path is gentle but exposed, marked by prayer flags and mani walls, and the sanctuary opens up in front of you.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Josep M. Gracia, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Machhapuchhre Base Camp
stops.narration:
Machhapuchhre Base Camp, 3,700 metres, at the foot of the north face of the mountain the Nepalis call the fishtail. The name is literal: machha, fish, and puchhre, tail, for the double summit that looks like a tail fin. The Gurung have their own name, Katasunkli, which means 'snowy fish mouth'. The mountain is 6,993 metres, just short of the magic seven thousand, and it is the most beautiful peak in the range by common consent, which is a dangerous thing to say about mountains.

It is also sacred, and it has never been officially climbed. In 1957 a British expedition led by Jimmy Roberts, the same man who had entered the sanctuary the year before, got permission from King Mahendra on one condition: nobody was to set foot on the summit. Wilfrid Noyce and David Cox climbed the north ridge to about 6,947 metres, 46 metres below the top, and turned back. Roberts then argued that the mountain should stay closed, and since the early 1960s no permit has been issued. There are rumours that a New Zealand climber, Bill Denz, reached the top illegally in the early 1980s; he died on Makalu before he could confirm it. The Gurung say the summit is Shiva's seat, and the plume of snow that blows off it is his incense. You do not need the theology to see why people leave it alone.

You are standing at the entrance to the sanctuary, in the gap between Hiunchuli and Machhapuchhre. Prayer flags cross the trail, mani walls of carved stone slabs line it, and the chortens, the mound-shaped reliquaries, mark the path. The 1957 expedition's base camp was here. So is your lunch.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk through. This is a lunch stop with a few lodges; food is expensive and cash is the only currency. Verify the price before you order.
stops.openingHours: The lodges are seasonal. Above this point the weather can close the trail at any time of year, and afternoon cloud is normal.
stops.accessibility: Open alpine ground, rough stone paths and prayer-flag obstacles; the altitude makes the short climbs feel long. Not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Do not treat this as the destination. It is 400 metres below base camp and the last easy place to turn around. If you are feeling the altitude here, go down, not up; base camp will still be there.
stops.nextStopDirections: From Machhapuchhre Base Camp the trail crosses the moraine, the rubble the glacier has pushed ahead of it, and climbs gently into the amphitheatre, about 3 km and one and a half to two hours to Annapurna Base Camp at 4,130 metres. Follow the prayer flags and the stone cairns; in cloud or fresh snow the path is easy to lose.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Jodhani.micky, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Annapurna Base Camp
stops.narration:
Annapurna Base Camp, 4,130 metres, and you are standing in the middle of the amphitheatre. The ring around you: Annapurna I at 8,091 metres, the tenth-highest mountain on Earth; Annapurna South at 7,219; Hiunchuli at 6,441; Gangapurna at 7,455; Annapurna III at 7,555; and Machhapuchhre at 6,993 behind you. The glacier is below the moraine, and the basin gets about seven hours of sun a day in midsummer because the walls are so high. The gorge you came up is the only way out.

The wall in front of you is the south face of Annapurna I, a 3,000-metre face of rock and ice and one of the hardest climbs in the world. It is not the route Herzog and Lachenal took in 1950; theirs was the north face, on the far side. The south face was climbed by Chris Bonington's team in 1970, and Ian Clough was killed by falling ice on that expedition. The memorial chortens near the lodges remember climbers who died here, including Anatoli Boukreev, the Kazakh guide who survived the 1996 Everest disaster and was killed on Annapurna on Christmas Day 1997, with the cameraman Dimitri Sobolev. Boukreev's chorten carries a line of his: 'Mountains are not stadiums where I satisfy my ambition to achieve, they are the cathedrals where I practice my religion.'

The Gurung held this basin sacred long before any of that. They believed it held gold left by the naga, the serpent-gods, and that the peaks were the homes of gods. Eggs and meat were traditionally forbidden here, and women were not allowed in. The sanctuary is still a sacred place to the people who live below it, and the lodges still depend on porters and mules from those villages for everything they eat.

Watch the sunrise. It hits Annapurna South first, then Annapurna I, then the glacier. Then have breakfast, because you are at 4,130 metres and the descent is the best treatment for altitude.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk in. The lodges here are the most expensive on the trek, cash only, and hot water is limited. Verify the room and meal prices before you settle; there is no ATM and no card machine.
stops.openingHours: The lodges operate in the trekking seasons and close in winter. The basin is open ground at all hours; do not walk the moraine alone in the dark or in a whiteout.
stops.accessibility: Rough moraine, stone paths and altitude. Not step-free, and the cold and thin air make the shortest walk feel like a climb.
stops.insiderTip: Sleep with your water bottle inside your sleeping bag or it freezes. Set an alarm for 30 minutes before sunrise, and watch from the moraine in front of the lodges rather than the crowded signboard. If you wake with a bad headache, nausea or breathlessness at rest, descend; do not wait for morning.
stops.nextStopDirections: The descent takes two days in the itinerary. Day 8 retraces the valley to Bamboo, about 14 km and six hours, past Machhapuchhre Base Camp, Deurali and Himalaya. Day 9 continues from Bamboo to Jhinu Danda, about 8.5 km and three to four hours, over the Sinuwa ridge and down to the hot springs. Going down is faster but harder on the knees; poles help.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Josep M. Gracia, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Jhinu Danda Hot Springs
stops.narration:
Jhinu Danda, 1,780 metres, and the last thing the trek owes you: three stone pools on the bank of the Modi Khola, 15 to 20 minutes below the village, sitting at 35 to 40 degrees Celsius. The water started as rain and snow. It sinks through fractures in the rock, is heated by the geothermal gradient as it goes down, picks up minerals, and rises again along a fault where the river has cut the valley. That is why the pools are here and not somewhere else, and why the water smells faintly of sulphur.

The path down from the village is a steep stone staircase, and the climb back up takes longer than you think, especially with legs that have just walked down from 4,130 metres. Bring a towel, a swimsuit and small notes. The pools are maintained by the community, and there is a small fee or donation, around NPR 200 to 300 when we checked; it moves. Rinse off before you get in, do not use soap, and take your rubbish out with you. This is a working river, not a spa.

The village itself is a Gurung settlement and a road head: the jeep track from Pokhara reaches the ridge below, which is why the trek ends here rather than at a trailhead in the middle of nowhere. From Jhinu the drive back to Pokhara is 2 to 3 hours on a rough mountain road, about 65 km, and from Pokhara the tourist bus to Kathmandu takes 6 to 7 hours, or a 25-minute flight if you have the budget.

End of the walk. You have come from 820 metres to 4,130 and back down, through terraced fields, rhododendron forest, bamboo and moraine, and you have slept in the houses of the people who farm the valley and carry its supplies. The water you are sitting in fell as snow on the Annapurnas, sank kilometres into the rock, and came back up here. That is the whole trek in one fact.
stops.entranceFeeNote: A small community fee or donation of around NPR 200 to 300 per person maintains the pools; some sources report no fixed ticket, so treat it as a donation and carry small notes. The ACAP permit is separate and already paid. Verify on the board at the entrance.
stops.openingHours: The pools are open through the trekking day, roughly 7am to 6pm, and sometimes later in peak season. They are busiest in the late afternoon; early morning is quietest.
stops.accessibility: A steep stone staircase down from the village, uneven and slippery when wet, with a longer climb back up. Not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Soak before dinner, not after, and leave yourself enough daylight for the climb back up. Carry a cold drink down with you; the contrast with the hot water is the whole pleasure. Bring a dry bag for your phone.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. From Jhinu Danda a private jeep or shared vehicle takes 2 to 3 hours on a rough road back to Pokhara, about 65 km. From Pokhara, the tourist bus to Kathmandu takes 6 to 7 hours, or a 25-minute flight. If you are walking out instead, the trail to Nayapul is about four to five hours, mostly downhill.
